blocks.content: Knowing the five principles is the easy part. Taking a real tangled class and cleaning it up without breaking anything is the part that actually pays your salary.
Good refactoring is not a heroic rewrite. It is a series of small, safe, boring moves, each one leaving the code working.
"Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing what it does."
In this lesson we take one messy class and walk it toward SOLID step by step. We will not change what it does. We will only change how it is shaped.
1. The starting point
Here is our patient. It works in production, and it is also a nightmare to change.
This one method validates, takes payment, persists, and notifies. It violates SRP, OCP, and DIP all at once. We will fix it in order, one principle per step.
2. Rule zero: lock the behaviour first
blocks.text: 2. Rule zero: lock the behaviour first

blocks.content: Before you move a single line, write tests that capture what the code does today. Refactoring is safe only when you can prove the behaviour did not change.
["Write tests for the current happy path and the obvious edge cases.","Run them and watch them pass against the messy code.","Refactor in small steps, running the tests after each one."]
items: Write tests for the current happy path and the obvious edge cases.
Run them and watch them pass against the messy code.
Refactor in small steps, running the tests after each one.

blocks.content: If you cannot tell whether a change broke something, you are not refactoring. You are gambling.
3. Step one: separate the jobs (SRP)
The first move is to give each responsibility its own home. We pull the four jobs out into focused classes.
Now OrderService stops doing the work itself and starts coordinating the specialists:

Each class now has one reason to change. A new email template never touches validation. This already reads far better, but notice OrderService still builds its own dependencies with new. We fix that next.
4. Step two: depend on abstractions (DIP)
Right now OrderService is glued to concrete classes. We introduce interfaces and pass the real implementations in through the constructor. This is dependency injection.
OrderService no longer knows or cares whether storage is MySQL or Postgres, or whether notifications go by email or SMS. The wins are immediate:

["You can swap the database by passing a different implementation.","You can test OrderService with fake in memory versions, no real database needed.","High level policy no longer depends on low level details."]
items: You can swap the database by passing a different implementation.
You can test OrderService with fake in memory versions, no real database needed.
High level policy no longer depends on low level details.

blocks.content: 5. Step three: open for extension (OCP)
The payment logic is still a growing if else chain. We replace it with a strategy: one interface, one implementation per payment type.
OrderService now accepts whatever payment method it is handed:

Adding crypto payments tomorrow means writing one new class. You never reopen OrderService, so you can never break the payment types that already work. The code is now open for extension and closed for modification.
6. Step four: keep substitution honest (LSP)
Strategies and interfaces only help if every implementation truly behaves like the type it claims to be. Watch out for the half implementation:

If a gift card cannot really pay yet, do not ship a class that throws when called. That reintroduces an LSP violation through the back door. Either implement it fully or do not register it as a usable PaymentMethod. Every implementation must honour the contract its interface promises.
7. Step five: keep interfaces lean (ISP)
As you extract interfaces, resist the urge to make one big interface that does everything. Keep each one focused on a single client need.
A class that only needs to save orders should not be forced to implement a search method it never uses. Small interfaces are easier to implement fully, which keeps LSP healthy too.
8. Before and after
We never changed what the code does. A customer still places an order and gets a confirmation. But the shape is completely different:

["Before: one class, one giant method, four hidden jobs, impossible to test in isolation.","After: small focused classes behind interfaces, wired together from the outside, each one testable and replaceable on its own."]
items: Before: one class, one giant method, four hidden jobs, impossible to test in isolation.
After: small focused classes behind interfaces, wired together from the outside, each one testable and replaceable on its own.

blocks.content: Refactoring did not make the code do more. It made the code easier to change. That is the whole point.
9. Common pitfalls
1. Refactoring without tests
This is how refactoring turns into rewriting bugs. If you cannot prove behaviour stayed the same, stop and write the tests first.
2. Doing it all in one giant commit
blocks.text: 2. Doing it all in one giant commit

blocks.content: A huge "cleaned everything" change is impossible to review and terrifying to merge. Make one small move at a time, commit, and keep the code green throughout.
3. Over refactoring
You can absolutely go too far. Five interfaces and three factories to send one email is not clean, it is noise. Apply SOLID where the code actually changes, not everywhere out of habit.
4. Chasing principles instead of pain
Do not refactor code just because it breaks a rule on paper. Refactor the parts that are genuinely hard to change. The goal is working software that is easy to evolve, not a perfect score.
10. Common questions
Where do I even start with a messy class? - Start with SRP. Pull the most obviously separate job into its own class first. Once responsibilities are split, DIP and OCP become much easier to apply.

Do I need every principle in every class? - No. SOLID is a toolbox, not a checklist. Reach for the principle that solves the pain you actually feel in that spot. Forcing all five everywhere just adds complexity.

How do I refactor code I am afraid to touch? - Wrap it in tests first, even rough ones that just pin the current output. Those tests become your safety net, and suddenly the scary code is safe to clean.
When should I stop refactoring? - Stop when the code is easy to change for the work in front of you. You are done when the next feature feels simple, not when the code is theoretically perfect.

You now have both halves of the skill. You can spot a SOLID violation by its smell, and you can refactor it away one safe step at a time. The same moves you used on OrderService work on any tangled class you will ever meet.
